h1: Catholic vs Orthodox: what is the difference?
searchTitle: Catholic vs Orthodox: The Real Differences, Plainly
description: The pope, the filioque and how doctrine grows: what really separates Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and the five things they hold together.
answer: Catholic and Orthodox Christians share the sacraments, the liturgy, the councils and the Fathers, and land in the same band on five of the Compass's six questions. What divides them is the pope's authority, one clause added to the Creed in the West, and how far doctrine may grow.
drawn: The Catholic rail draws the church in communion with Rome, the Latin rite and the twenty-three Eastern Catholic churches alike. The Orthodox rail draws the Eastern Orthodox communion, Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian, Antiochian and the rest; the Oriental Orthodox churches, which parted earlier still, are a separate communion and are not drawn here.
common: Both hold that the bread and the cup at the altar are the body and blood of Christ, and neither will call the Supper a symbol. Both baptise infants. In an Orthodox parish the baby is chrismated at the same service, anointed with holy oil as the East's form of confirmation, and is given communion from that day on.

Neither reads the Bible on its own. Scripture here belongs to the church that recognised which books belong in it, and its meaning has been kept by the creeds, by the councils the whole church received, and by the Fathers, the teachers of its first centuries.
Sunday is a liturgy rather than a programme in both: a fixed order, a calendar of feasts and fasts, readings appointed in advance, and the Eucharist at the centre of the day.

Both still expect the Holy Spirit to heal and to startle. Neither tradition ever announced that He had stopped, so saints, wonders and prayers answered for the sick belong to ordinary church life rather than to a movement inside it.
Israel and the church are one people of God on both sides. Neither expects a rapture, and neither reads Revelation with a seven-year timetable in hand.

differences.heading: How grace and free will fit together
differences.a: Catholic teaching starts where Orthodoxy does: nothing at the beginning is earned. The Catechism calls grace the free and undeserved help God gives, and Trent taught that justification begins with grace running ahead of anything a person does. But Trent also condemned the idea that the will is purely passive and cannot refuse its consent, and that refusal is why the Catholic marker sits a little short of the Orthodox one. Centuries of Western argument, first with Pelagius and later with the Reformers, left Catholics stating it as a careful balance: God moves first, and the person can still say no.
differences.b: The East has one word for it, synergy, from the Greek for working together, and it is older than the Western argument rather than a compromise between its sides. God's grace does everything, and the person must genuinely cooperate with it; the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 answered a Calvinist confession by saying God predestines according to His foreknowledge of how each person will use their freedom. Behind that stands theosis: salvation is not only being forgiven but being drawn into the very life of God.
differences.plain: Both say God moves first and that you can still refuse Him; the East never framed it as a contest between God's grace and your will in the first place.

beyond_the_compass.heading: The pope
beyond_the_compass.text: This is the difference the six questions do not reach. Catholics hold that the bishop of Rome is Peter's successor with real authority over the whole church, and the First Vatican Council defined in 1870 that he teaches without error when he speaks solemnly on faith and morals. The Orthodox communion has no such office: its churches govern themselves, its patriarchs are equals, and the Patriarch of Constantinople is first in honour rather than in command. Orthodox Christians grant Rome an honoured place in the undivided church. What they deny is that it ever carried command over the rest.

beyond_the_compass.heading: The filioque
beyond_the_compass.text: One Latin word, in the one text both sides say every Sunday. The Nicene Creed as the councils wrote it says the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; the West added that He proceeds from the Father and the Son, which in Latin is filioque. Orthodox Christians object twice over, to the teaching and to the fact that a creed settled by an ecumenical council was altered without one. Catholics answer that the addition guards the Son's place and makes no second source inside God.

beyond_the_compass.heading: How far doctrine may grow
beyond_the_compass.text: Orthodoxy recognises seven ecumenical councils, the last at Nicaea in 787, and holds that the faith was delivered whole and is guarded rather than added to. The Catholic Church has gone on defining: the Immaculate Conception in 1854, papal infallibility in 1870, the Assumption of Mary in 1950. Catholics see those as the same faith made explicit, which is what development of doctrine means. Orthodox Christians see the defining itself as the problem, since not one of them came from a council both halves of the church attended.

story: The two halves of the church did not fall out on a date. They drifted. Greek East and Latin West prayed in different languages, answered to different capitals, and by the ninth century were arguing about the Creed and about how far Rome's authority reached. In 1054 a papal legation and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, and that is the year in every textbook.

What made the break stick came later. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and installed a Latin ruler in a Greek city. Reunion was signed at the Council of Florence in 1439 by an emperor and bishops who needed Western help against the Turks, and the faithful at home would not have it. Constantinople fell in 1453 anyway.

The anathemas of 1054 have been gone since 7 December 1965, when a joint declaration of Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I was read out at the same hour in Rome and in Istanbul, committing them to oblivion. The two churches are still not in communion. A Catholic and an Orthodox Christian who stand together on five of these six questions still cannot receive at one another's altars.
on_a_sunday: A Catholic Mass runs under an hour: pews, a printed order, two readings, a psalm and a Gospel set years in advance so that Manila and Munich hear the same one, a homily, then communion in a line or at a rail. Kneeling is common and there is holy water at the door. An Orthodox Divine Liturgy is sung almost end to end, usually unaccompanied, in a church covered with icons and thick with incense. Most people stand, the priest chooses almost nothing, babies are carried to the chalice, and everyone leaves with a piece of blessed bread.
did_you_know: Catholic does not mean Latin. The communion is made of twenty-four self-governing churches: the Latin one most Westerners picture, and twenty-three Eastern Catholic churches with their own liturgies, their own canon law and, in many of them, married priests.
